procedural_history.originating_court: District Magistrate, Tanjore (in pursuance of 2 notifications (G. 0. Mis. 1054, Home, dated 28th March, 1948, and G. 0. Mis. 3422, dated 15th September, 1948) issued by the State of Madras)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Conditions in the cinema license imposed by the District Magistrate, Tanjore, specifically condition No. 4(a) and special condition No. 3.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Civil Applications Nos. 409, 410, 411 and 780 of 1951 in the High Court of Judicature at Bombay. The High Court order was dated 6th December, 1951.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed under article 132(1) and 133(1)(c) of the Constitution of India from the Judgment and Order dated 24th August, 1951, of the Madras High Court in Civil Miscellaneous Petition No. 5744 of 1951 and the Judgment and Order dated the 6th December, 1951. of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in Civil Applications Nos. 409, 410, 411 and 780 of 1951. The appellant challenged the conditions as violating his fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that condition No. 4(a) and special condition No. 3 imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right of the licensee to carry on his business and were void as they infringed the fundamental right of the appellant guaranteed to him under Art. 19( 1) (g) of the Constitution.

directions: Condition 4(a) and special condition 3 expressed as they are at present are void and have no legal effect as against the fundamental right of the appellant under article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
The appellant will get his costs from the respondent in this Court and in the Court below.

issue.issue_text: Whether condition No. 4(a) and special condition No. 3, imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right of the licensee to carry on his business and were void as they infringed the fundamental right of the appellant guaranteed to him under Art. 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.

facts: The appellant, a cinema owner, was granted a license that included certain conditions imposed by the State of Madras.
Condition 4(a) compelled the licensee to exhibit approved films of a length and for a duration as directed by the government.
Special condition 3 required the licensee to exhibit a minimum of 2,000 feet of approved films at the beginning of each performance.
law: The issue was whether these conditions constituted "reasonable restrictions" on the fundamental right to carry on a business, as guaranteed by Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
application: The Court analyzed condition 4(a) and found that it gave the government "unregulated discretion" because it did not specify any maximum length for the film or the duration for which it had to be shown. This meant the government could compel the cinema to show a film so long that it would consume the entire performance time, potentially leading to the "total extinction of the business itself."

The Court found special condition 3 to be similarly flawed. While it set a minimum length of 2,000 feet, it gave "no indication of the maximum." This left the government with "unrestrained and unfettered" discretion to compel the showing of a much longer film (e.g., 10,000 or 12,000 feet), which would effectively push out the film the licensee intended to show.

The Court concluded that because both conditions were couched in such wide language and lacked any guiding principles or upper limits, they operated harshly and amounted to an "unjustifiable interference" with the licensee's business, savouring more of an "imposition than a restriction."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that both condition 4(a) and special condition 3 imposed unreasonable restrictions on the licensee's right to carry on his business. The conditions were declared void as they infringed the fundamental right guaranteed to the appellant under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949 (Bombay Act LXII of 1949) can be questioned on the ground that it takes away or abridges the fundamental rights conferred by the Constitution of India.

facts: The validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949 was challenged.
The basis for the challenge was that the Act allegedly took away or abridged the fundamental rights conferred by the Constitution of India.
law: Article 31-B was inserted into the Constitution by the First Amendment in 1951.
Article 31-B protects laws that are specifically enumerated in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution from being challenged on the ground that they violate fundamental rights.
application: The Court noted that the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, was specifically listed as item number 4 in the Ninth Schedule.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that because the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, was included in the Ninth Schedule, Article 31-B of the Constitution prevented it from being questioned on the ground that it abridged or took away any fundamental rights. Therefore, the challenge to the Act's validity was rejected.

facts: The validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949 (Bombay Act LXII of 1949) was challenged.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that because the Bombay Act LXII of 1949 was included in the Ninth Schedule, its validity could not be challenged under s. 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935, due to the protection granted by Article 31-B of the Constitution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A condition imposed on a license which vests the government with unregulated discretion to determine the extent of an obligation, without specifying any limits, imposes an unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right to carry on a business under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution and is therefore void.
obiter: The court expressed no opinion on whether the notifications and conditions were beyond the competence of the government or whether they violated the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that condition No. 4(a) and special condition No. 3 were void because they imposed unreasonable restrictions on the licensee's fundamental right to carry on his business under Article 19(1)(g). The conditions were unreasonable because they vested the Government with unregulated, unrestrained, and unfettered discretion. For condition 4(a), neither the length of the film nor the time for which it may be shown was specified, giving the Government an 'unregulated discretion' that 'may lead to the loss or total extinction of the business itself.' For special condition 3, by setting a minimum length for a compulsory film but giving 'no indication of the maximum,' the discretion of the authority was 'unrestrained and unfettered and must lead to an unjustificable interference with the right of the licensee to carry on his business.' The court found that a condition 'couched in such wide language' savours 'more of the nature of an imposition than a restriction.'
legal_tests_applied: Whether the impugned conditions amount to 'reasonable restrictions' within the meaning of article 19(6).
policy_considerations: A condition that grants a licensing authority unrestrained and unfettered discretion, with no guiding principle, can operate so harshly on a business that it may lead to its total extinction, and therefore cannot be regarded as a reasonable restriction on the fundamental right to carry on that business.
